Volume 07 · Chapter 08

Managerial accounting and cost decisions

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c07

By the endUse contribution margins and relevant costs for operational decisions.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can use contribution margins and relevant costs to choose an operating plan, test break-even claims, reconcile overhead assignments, and evaluate special orders or outsourcing when capacity is scarce. Read taxes, accruals and earnings quality; retain the cash-versus-expense distinctions and the inventory and asset mechanics of Chapters 3–4. Our decisions deliberately use supplied before-tax costs without tax or working-capital timing. A real decision must restore any timing, tax, risk or financing effects that differ across alternatives.

The useful question is not simply “What does this product cost?” It is “Which costs and benefits change under this decision, over this period, and what else could use the resources?” A full-cost report answers a measurement question. It need not answer the incremental decision.

Model and units. Meridian Components is an original fictional one-month business. All amounts are CU, fictional currency units, not kCU. Output consists of whole units. All production is sold and collected in the month; inputs and capacity services are consumed and cash-paid then. The main case has no opening or closing inventory, receivables, payables, owned depreciable assets, debt, tax or owner flows. Opening cash and equity are 20,000. Fixed monthly service pools are cash commitments within the stated capacity; no fixed payment disappears merely because fewer units are made. The separate inventory and make-or-buy examples state their own facts. These are internal decision models, not current financial-reporting compliance rules or observed industry cost estimates.

1. Cost labels require an object, a driver and a horizon

A cost object is the product, customer, job, department or decision whose cost we want to examine. A cost directly traceable to a department may be indirect to each unit made there. Direct versus indirect concerns traceability. Fixed versus variable concerns behavior with a specified activity over a stated range and period. The classifications need not coincide: a dedicated designer's monthly salary can be direct to one product but fixed for this month. Electricity shared by several products can be indirect and variable with machine use.

For the simple one-product model C(q) = F + vq, F is total fixed cost per period, v is variable cost per unit and q is units produced and sold. F ≥ 0 and v ≥ 0 are supplied constants within a relevant range. For q > 0, average total cost is F/q + v: the fixed-cost amount per unit falls as q rises, even though total F has not fallen. At q = 0, an average cost per unit is undefined. A mixed cost has fixed and variable elements; a step cost jumps when another block of capacity is needed. Khan's MIT cost-terminology lecture develops these distinctions and separates contribution margin from gross margin.

The relevant range is the domain in which the assumed price, resource requirements, variable costs and fixed commitments remain credible. Producing beyond a machine limit may require overtime, another shift or subcontracting. A constant marginal cost cannot be extrapolated across that change without evidence. Likewise, two months of cost observations do not identify a causal cost law if input prices, quality, product mix and maintenance conditions also changed. A fitted line from accounting data can describe an association; engineering records, contracts and an identified comparison are needed to support a decision forecast.

Separate behavior from relevance
CostBehavior in a stated rangeRelevance to a decision
Materials newly purchased only for accepted unitsVariable with output in our caseAvoidable when those units are not made
A monthly service contract already committedFixed for the monthUnchanged across the month's feasible plans
A cancellable supervisor contract needed only for one batchFixed for that batchAvoidable if that batch is outsourced
Historical design expenditure already paid, with no refundA past cost, not a future activity responseSunk; not changed by accepting the new order
Contribution forgone on a displaced regular orderDepends on the alternative use of capacityOpportunity cost, even without a separate ledger payment

Relevant costs are the future consequences that differ across feasible alternatives. A fixed amount can be relevant if avoidable; a cost called variable may already be committed for the decision at hand. Sunk expenditure is unchanged by today's choice, but an existing asset's future resale proceeds or an inventory item's alternative use can be relevant. For these distinctions see the actual OpenStax treatment of differential, sunk and opportunity costs. Do not infer avoidability from the column in which an accountant placed a cost.

2. Contribution margin and break-even are conditional statements

For a unit selling at p with total variable cost v, unit contribution is m = p − v. Include every variable cost affected by that sale, including selling or distribution costs when applicable. With all output sold and no inventory timing, operating profit is π(q) = pq − vq − F = mq − F. Contribution first covers the period's fixed commitments; any excess is profit. Gross margin, which subtracts cost of goods sold, can mix fixed manufacturing costs with variable costs and exclude variable selling expenses. It is not automatically m.

If m > 0: continuous break-even q* = F/m.
For whole units: smallest nonloss quantity = ceiling(F/m), provided it is feasible.
For target profit T ≥ 0: q ≥ (F + T)/m, again subject to demand and capacity.

The result follows by solving mq − F = 0 or mq − F ≥ T. If F > 0 and m ≤ 0, no nonnegative quantity breaks even in this constant-cost model. If F = 0 and m = 0, every feasible quantity has zero profit; if F = 0 and m < 0, only q = 0 does. A positive-margin break-even quantity outside capacity does not become attainable because the division produced a number. Step costs require solving and checking each interval, including the cost jumps.

For multiple products, profit is Σmjqj − F. Without a fixed mix there is generally a set of zero-profit combinations, not a unique “number of units.” Specify a bundle containing bj units of each product. Its contribution M = Σmjbj gives profit zM − F for z bundles. With M > 0, z* = F/M. A unit mix and a revenue-share mix are different inputs: do not average contribution percentages using unit shares.

Worked example 1: Meridian's baseline and fixed sales mix

One-month product facts
Per unitStandard SPrecision P
Price / variable cash cost, CU100 / 70160 / 100
Contribution, CU3060
Machine hours25
Maximum monthly demand, units8050
Units per setup batch, at most102

The facility supplies 300 machine-hours and 30 setups. A partial batch requires a whole setup; products cannot share a setup. Machine hours exclude setup work, which has its own separate capacity measure. Fixed monthly cash pools are machine support 1,800, setup support 900 and common facility service 300, totaling 3,000. Variable unit costs exclude these pools. Within these limits the pools are committed, including when idle.

A baseline plan of S = 60 and P = 24 uses 2×60 + 5×24 = 240 hours and 6 + 12 = 18 setups. Revenue is 6,000 + 3,840 = 9,840; variable cost is 4,200 + 2,400 = 6,600; contribution is 3,240 and profit is 240. Under the supplied all-cash, no-inventory conventions, operating cash also increases by 240. Ending cash and equity are both 20,240. The pre-funded opening equity is not current revenue.

Now restrict sales to bundles of five S and two P. Bundle revenue is 820, variable cost 550 and contribution 270. Break-even is 3,000/270 = 100/9 bundles, about 11.111. Whole bundles require at least 12, producing the baseline 60 S and 24 P, with profit 240. Eleven bundles contribute only 2,970 and lose 30. Twelve bundles fit both resources and the demand caps. Continuous break-even revenue is 820×100/9 = 82,000/9 CU; the contribution ratio is 270/820 = 27/82, not the arithmetic average of the two products' margin percentages.

This calculation assumes the 5:2 mix is maintained. It does not say that the baseline is the most profitable feasible plan. Indeed, if mix is flexible and more orders are available up to the stated caps, the next capacity example improves it. An accounting break-even result describes a conditional volume requirement, not a market-demand forecast.

3. Allocation reconciles a pool; it does not prove avoidability

An overhead pool groups indirect resource costs. A driver measures the activity used to assign that pool to cost objects. For a specified denominator D > 0, rate r = pool/D and assigned cost for object j is r dj. If Σdj = D, the assignments exhaust the pool. If D instead measures practical capacity K and actual usage is below K, cost assigned to actual use plus cost of unused capacity equals the supplied pool. These are accounting identities once the pool and driver are chosen; the driver's economic appropriateness requires evidence.

Separate pools can distinguish products that consume very different activities. Setup counts may explain demands on a setup team better than sales value, while machine hours can describe equipment-service use. Common costs without a defensible product-level driver can remain visible at facility level. MIT's product-costing lecture discusses pool homogeneity, driver selection and denominator effects. More categories also require data and maintenance: apparent precision is not a reason to invent a causal driver.

Activity-based costing (ABC) traces products' use of activities, then assigns the related resource costs. Our version uses practical-capacity rates and reports unused capacity separately. The underlying resource-supply logic is explained in the actual Kaplan–Anderson HBS excerpt. We supply the capacities as case facts; we do not apply a universal percentage of theoretical capacity. Nor do we claim that an allocated 30 CU per setup is an avoidable 30 CU payment whenever one setup is removed.

Worked example 2: a product loss that depends on the allocation

Take Meridian's baseline 60 S and 24 P. A retrospective single-rate report allocates all 3,000 of fixed costs by the actual 240 machine-hours: 12.5 CU per hour. Each product used 120 hours, so each receives 1,500. Product contribution less assigned fixed cost becomes 1,800 − 1,500 = 300 for S and 1,440 − 1,500 = −60 for P. The product margins sum to the correct company profit 240.

Now retain resource distinctions. The practical-capacity rate for machine support is 1,800/300 = 6 CU per hour; setup support is 900/30 = 30 CU per setup. These denominators describe resources supplied, not the lower baseline usage. Common facility service 300 remains unassigned to products.

Baseline ABC pool reconciliation, CU
PoolAssigned to SAssigned to PUnused / commonTotal
Machine support120×6 = 720120×6 = 72060×6 = 360 unused1,800
Setup support6×30 = 18012×30 = 36012×30 = 360 unused900
Common facility service00300 common300
Total9001,0801,0203,000

Product margins after assignment are 1,800 − 900 = 900 and 1,440 − 1,080 = 360. Subtract unused-capacity cost 720 and common cost 300: 900 + 360 − 720 − 300 = 240. No company expense vanished. The second report makes resource use and unused supply visible; it has not discovered 1,020 of instantly cancellable payments.

Dropping all 24 P units with no replacement sales would remove contribution 1,440 while the 3,000 commitment remains. Profit would fall from 240 to −1,200, despite the first report's allocated P loss of 60. If freed resources support other sales or an actual contract can be cancelled, include those changes explicitly. Removing a column and reallocating its overhead to S is not evidence of a saving.

The single-rate calculation is deliberately retrospective. A predetermined rate would use its stated budget denominator instead. At zero actual machine-hours the retrospective rate is undefined; a practical-capacity report can still show the full supplied pool as unused. Rising reported unit cost during a demand slump can therefore reflect a shrinking denominator rather than more cash paid per resource unit.

4. Capacity creates an opportunity cost

With only one divisible resource, positive contributions, constant requirements and separable demand caps, contribution per scarce-resource unit helps rank uses. For Meridian, S contributes 30/2 = 15 CU per machine-hour, while P contributes 60/5 = 12. Ranking by contribution per product would favor P because 60 exceeds 30, but would ignore its larger resource requirement. The general bottleneck intuition appears in OpenStax's constrained-resource chapter. Integer quantities, setups, joint sales, several resources or minimum commitments can defeat a simple ranking rule; write the feasible set and verify the result.

Worked example 3: a global optimum and its limits

Let x be S units and y be P units. The month's problem is to maximize 30x + 60y − 3,000 over nonnegative integers satisfying x ≤ 80, y ≤ 50, 2x + 5y ≤ 300, and ceiling(x/10) + ceiling(y/2) ≤ 30. Zero units require zero setups. These constraints include demand as well as production technology.

Making 80 S uses 160 hours. The remaining 140 hours allow 28 P. This plan uses 8 + 14 = 22 setups, so it is feasible. To prove it is globally optimal, rather than merely plausible, rewrite every feasible plan's contribution:

30x + 60y = 12(2x + 5y) + 6x ≤ 12×300 + 6×80 = 4,080.

The bound uses only constraints every feasible plan satisfies. The candidate (80,28) attains 4,080, proving global optimality even before checking other plans. Equality requires both x = 80 and 2x + 5y = 300, hence y = 28: the optimum is unique here, including in the continuous relaxation. Profit is 1,080, revenue 12,480 and variable costs 8,400. Ending cash and equity are 21,080.

The practical-capacity ABC assignments now become S: 160×6 + 8×30 = 1,200; P: 140×6 + 14×30 = 1,260. Unused machine cost is zero, unused setup cost is 8×30 = 240, and common cost remains 300. The reconciliation is 1,200 + 1,260 + 240 + 300 = 3,000. Product margins 1,200 and 420 less the remaining 540 also give profit 1,080.

How much is another hour worth?

For five extra usable machine-hours, holding demand and setup capacity fixed and before paying for the extra hours, (80,29) is feasible and adds 60 of contribution. The same bound with 305 hours proves it optimal. An all-in fee of 50 for those five hours would leave a gain of 10; a fee of 70 would not. The original fixed pools cover only their stated service capacity: the extra-capacity fee is a separate relevant cost.

The familiar 12 CU per hour is a local value from the divisible relaxation while S's demand cap and machine capacity bind and other constraints permit the adjustment. With whole units, one added hour from 300 to 301 produces no higher contribution: (80,28) and (78,29) both yield 4,080, and enumeration verifies that no feasible pair beats them. Five hours unlock a full additional P. A continuous slope need not equal every one-unit change in an integer problem.

It also cannot be extrapolated indefinitely. At 400 machine-hours the setup constraint becomes decisive. Since x/10 + y/2 ≤ ceiling(x/10) + ceiling(y/2) ≤ 30, we have y ≤ 60 − x/5. Consequently 30x + 60y ≤ 3,600 + 18x ≤ 5,040. The plan (80,44) attains this bound, uses 380 hours and all 30 setups, and has profit 2,040 before any fee for expansion. Another machine-hour then has zero value with these demand and setup restrictions. This second global bound explains why the active bottleneck matters.

A special order: compare complete feasible alternatives

A new customer offers 85 CU each for ten S-like units. Each costs 70 in new variable cash and uses two machine-hours; the order requires one separate setup and an extra external preparation/delivery payment of 40. That 40 is outside the committed pools and unit variable cost. Assume no cannibalization of regular prices, no quality change, no later price commitment and prompt payment.

In an idle-order-book context, regular sales are fixed at the baseline 60 S and 24 P, with no additional regular demand that month. There are 60 unused hours and 12 unused setups. The order fits; incremental profit is 10(85 − 70) − 40 = 110. Its break-even quote is 70 + 40/10 = 74 per unit. These demand facts differ from the flexible-mix optimization context.

In the busy context, regular demand is available up to 80 S and 50 P, so the alternative without the order is the optimal (80,28). Reserving 20 hours and one setup leaves regular capacity of 280 hours and 29 setups. Reoptimization gives (80,24), losing four P contributions, or 240. The order's increment is 150 − 40 − 240 = −130. Its break-even quote is 70 + (40 + 240)/10 = 98. A positive own contribution of 150 is insufficient when it displaces more valuable production. The opportunity cost is computed from the best feasible alternative, not from a historical overhead allocation.

At the quoted threshold the firm is financially indifferent under the supplied assumptions; a strict preference needs a higher quote or another benefit. If the customer also causes credit exposure, warranty risk, rush costs, future price spillovers or loss of regular customers, their consequences belong in the comparison. Do not subtract lost contribution twice by both reducing regular sales in a complete scenario and adding the same amount again as an opportunity-cost expense.

5. Make-or-buy requires an avoidability and alternative-use map

Build two future scenarios with the same required output and quality. For each cost, state whether it changes, why it changes and when the cash settles. Include avoidable batch costs, buying-related inspection and transport, and the value of resources released. Keep common unchanged amounts out of the difference, but retain them when explaining total firm profit. A purchase price below allocated full cost is not sufficient evidence for outsourcing.

Worked example 4: an apparent saving reverses when capacity is idle

This is a separate next-month component decision for Meridian, not an extra use of the main case's 300 hours. Exactly 100 acceptable components are needed under either alternative. Internal variable cash cost is 14 each. A batch-supervision contract of 300 can be cancelled without penalty if all components are bought. Book depreciation of 500 and allocated common cash cost of 200 do not change under either choice; the equipment remains owned, has no alternative sale in this case, and taxes are absent. The supplier quotes 17 per accepted unit, and buying requires an additional inspection payment of 100. Assume identical acceptable quality and delivery.

The relevant make cost is 100×14 + 300 = 1,700; buying costs 100×17 + 100 = 1,800. If the released capacity has no alternative use, make is better by 100. The full accounting make cost 1,400 + 300 + 500 + 200 = 2,400, or 24 per unit, would misleadingly suggest that a quote of 17 necessarily saves 7 each. It ignores unchanged costs and the additional buying cost.

Now suppose buying frees capacity that can earn a supplied 500 of net contribution on an alternative job. The 500 is after all additional costs of that job, including any setup or delivery; it excludes the unchanged common amounts. Relative to making, buying changes operating cash by 1,700 − 1,800 + 500 = +400, so buy is preferred. Equivalently compare make's 1,700 plus opportunity cost 500 with buy's 1,800. Use one method or the other, not both.

The maximum supplier quote p that leaves buying weakly preferable solves 100p + 100 ≤ 1,700 + 500, giving p ≤ 21 CU per unit. Without the alternative job it is p ≤ 16. These thresholds require the promised capacity use, avoidable supervision and quality to be real. A late delivery, a noncancellable contract or a merely hoped-for alternative sale changes the answer.

A decision report should show sensitivity to the uncertain inputs rather than burying them in an average full cost. For a risk-neutral comparison, supplied state probabilities can produce an expected incremental cost. Expected profit alone does not prove that every cash-shortfall state is fundable, that specifications are met or that costs imposed on others are acceptable. The earlier microeconomics chapters distinguish private incentives from social consequences; a business ledger need not include every external effect.

6. Inventory can change reported profit without changing customer cash

Our main case equated production and sales. If they differ, an absorption report can retain fixed manufacturing cost in unsold inventory, whereas a variable-cost management report charges that fixed amount to the period. For the following comparison, both reports use the same prices, physical production, cash payments and valid unsold units. This is a stipulated measurement bridge, not a statement that every external-reporting framework accepts both presentations. MIT's lecture on production incentives explains why inventory-based performance measures need scrutiny.

Suppose a separate plant produces 100 units, its stipulated normal monthly capacity, and sells 80 at 60 each. Variable manufacturing cost is 30 per unit made; fixed manufacturing cost is 1,000, with an applied rate of 1,000/100 = 10 per unit. Variable selling cost is 5 per unit sold and fixed administration is 200. There is no beginning inventory, unfinished work, abnormal waste, write-down, production-volume variance, tax or working-capital lag. All costs are cash-paid and all sales collected. The remaining 20 units are expected to be sold and meet the stipulated carrying-value conditions.

Same physical operation, two internal profit presentations, CU
ItemAbsorption presentationVariable-cost presentation
Revenue4,8004,800
Manufacturing cost of sold units80×40 = 3,20080×30 = 2,400
Separate fixed manufacturing period charge01,000
Selling cost / administration400 / 200400 / 200
Profit1,000800
Ending inventory800600

Cash from operations is 4,800 − 3,000 − 1,000 − 400 − 200 = 200 under either presentation. The profit-to-cash bridges are 1,000 − 800 = 200 and 800 − 600 = 200. The 200 profit difference is the fixed manufacturing cost retained in ending inventory: 10×20. Neither selling/admin costs nor a fictional cash saving is put into the stock.

More generally, with a consistent fixed manufacturing rate a, matched opening inventory layers and no relevant variances or write-downs, absorption profit minus variable-cost profit equals a times the increase in inventory units. Equivalently it is fixed manufacturing cost deferred at closing minus such cost released from opening inventory. When layers or rates differ, use the cost amounts, not a single rate times net units. The identity comes from the different timing of the same fixed cost. It is not a license to keep an obsolete rate, capitalize abnormal waste or manufacture goods with no credible use merely to meet an earnings target. Pair profit with sales, inventory aging, cash and capacity evidence.

7. Use the reproducible benchmark as a decision audit

Download the original operating inputs, exact standard-library Python benchmark and execution and experiment guide. Keep them together and run python3 v07-c08-analysis.py. No installation, network access or persistent output is required. The script uses exact fractions and tests every whole-unit pair within the small demand caps; all ties are retained. A detailed allocation is shown for the first optimal plan, while the choice list preserves any other maximizers.

The baseline has 3,493 feasible pairs among 81×51 = 4,131 candidates. Enumeration is a global verification here because that list contains every admissible integer quantity pair; it is not a claim that an arbitrary large production problem should be solved by brute force. The analytic bound provides a second, differently structured proof of the baseline optimum. The program separately checks machine hours and rounded-up batches, recomputes the regular plan after reserving special-order capacity, and reconciles product assignments, unused pools and company profit.

Inputs retain the stated one-month CU/hour/batch contract. Finite positive capacities and batch sizes are required; total committed fixed cost is positive in this lab, and prices and variable costs may yield positive, zero or negative contribution. A zero-output plan remains feasible. No break-even is reported for a nonpositive-contribution mix with positive fixed cost. A supplied baseline that exceeds resources or demand is rejected. Changing a capacity input supplies a new hypothetical capacity budget; it does not obtain a real expansion for free. Any actual expansion payment must enter the decision comparison.

Before interpreting a result, verify the demanded quantities, payment terms, cost commitments, driver evidence, quality requirements and usable capacity. A solver cannot establish those facts. Its output is conditional on them. The main model omits uncertainty to make the logic visible; a sensitivity exercise then tells you which inputs matter enough to investigate.

Exercises

All amounts are CU. Unless changed below, amounts are before tax, current revenues and costs settle in the period, and unrelated costs remain unchanged. Give the relevant calculation and the decision's assumptions, not just a number.

  1. A single-product service sells for 10 per unit. For integer output 0 ≤ q ≤ 100, total cost is 600 + 4q. For 101 ≤ q ≤ 160, an additional capacity block makes total cost 900 + 4q. The initial 600 is committed. Find every integer break-even output and the sign of profit in each interval. If demand is at most 120, choose the globally profit-maximizing output and explain why positive unit contribution does not justify producing all 120.
  2. Product A sells for 80 with variable cost 50; B sells for 110 with variable cost 60. Fixed cost is 2,100 and capacity is sufficient for every quantity requested here. Calculate continuous and whole-bundle break-even for a unit mix of two A to one B, and then one A to two B. Compare profit at 60 total units for the two corresponding mixes. Explain why the original unit-count break-even cannot simply be reused after the mix changes.
  3. A machine-support pool of 1,800 supplies practical capacity of 900 hours; a setup pool of 600 supplies 20 setups. X uses 300 hours and two setups, while Y uses 450 hours and 12 setups. Compute the rates, assignments to X and Y, unused cost in each pool and full reconciliation. All supplied pool payments are committed for the month. Does Y's assigned overhead equal the immediate cash saving from removing Y with no change in contracts? State what further evidence would make a cost reduction credible.
  4. Keep Meridian's original unit margins, demand and 30 setups. An external service offers ten extra usable machine-hours, increasing capacity from 300 to 310, for an all-in fee of 150; it causes no other cost or quality change. Find and prove the best expanded plan, gross contribution improvement and net benefit of purchasing the expansion. Separately find the global optimum if 400 machine-hours were available before any expansion fee, and explain why the original 12-per-hour value fails across the full increase.
  5. A different firm receives a special order for six units at 45 each. New variable cost is 18 each and the order adds a preparation payment of 36. It uses 12 hours. All current capacity is occupied; accepting it displaces exactly three regular units with contribution 40 each, with no feasible better rearrangement. Compute incremental profit and the break-even special quote. Recalculate the decision if a known delivery penalty of 20 is also triggered. Contrast with a genuinely idle case with no displaced regular sales.
  6. A firm needs 50 components. Making costs 8 in new variable cash per unit plus an avoidable batch payment of 200. Depreciation 150 and a common cash charge 100 are unchanged; a design payment of 80 was made last year and is nonrefundable. Buying costs 13 per unit plus shipping of 100. It releases resources that can earn 180 of net contribution, after all added costs. Find the relevant make and buy costs, buying's net advantage and maximum acceptable unit quote. Then suppose buying also permits a cash sale of an otherwise retained machine for 30, with no tax, selling fee or change in the 180 contribution. Recalculate the advantage and quote ceiling; explain why the machine's past book cost is not substituted for its sale proceeds.
  7. A separate plant produces 120 units, its normal capacity, and sells 90 for 50 each. Variable manufacturing cost is 20 per unit produced, fixed manufacturing cost 1,200, variable selling cost 4 per unit sold and fixed administration 300. There is no beginning inventory, variance, write-down, tax or payment lag. Under the stipulated absorption method use fixed manufacturing rate 1,200/120; under variable costing charge all fixed manufacturing cost currently. Reconcile profit, closing inventory and operating cash in both presentations. Explain the profit difference without claiming additional customer cash.
  8. Return to Worked example 4's buying advantage of 400 before new risks. Stipulate a risk-neutral monetary comparison: with probability 1/4 buying causes an additional rework payment of 1,200; otherwise rework costs zero. Buying also causes an expected external cost of 150 borne by nearby residents and absent from the firm's accounts. Compute the expected private incremental benefit and the incremental net social benefit counting that harm. The purchase contract separately requires a certified quality test, which the supplier has not yet documented. Does the positive private expectation establish that buying is an admissible choice? State two additional operational facts that an allocation report alone cannot establish.
Complete solutions and decision boundaries
  1. Profit is 6q − 600 for 0 ≤ q ≤ 100 and 6q − 900 for 101 ≤ q ≤ 160. The break-even quantities are 100 and 150, each in the branch used to calculate it. Profit is negative for 0–99, zero at 100, negative again for 101–149, zero at 150 and positive for 151–160. On each branch profit increases with q, but the jump to the second branch reduces profit: q = 101 yields −294. With demand capped at 120, only branch maxima q = 100 and q = 120 need comparison, giving 0 versus −180. Thus q = 100 uniquely maximizes profit; q = 0 still loses the committed 600. Producing 20 extra units brings 120 of contribution but triggers 300 of additional cost. Ignoring that step would use the constant-cost model outside its relevant range.
  2. Unit margins are 30 and 50. A (2,1) bundle contributes 110, so continuous break-even is 210/11 bundles, and whole bundles require 20, producing 40 A and 20 B with profit 100. A (1,2) bundle contributes 130, so continuous break-even is 210/13 bundles; the first nonloss whole plan is 17, producing 17 A and 34 B with profit 110. At 60 total units, the first mix is (40,20) with profit 40×30 + 20×50 − 2,100 = 100. The second is (20,40), with profit 500. The same unit count carries different total contribution because the composition changed. No fixed-cost allocation to individual products is needed for the bundle calculation.
  3. Rates are 2 per hour and 30 per setup. X receives 300×2 + 2×30 = 660; Y receives 450×2 + 12×30 = 1,260. Unused machine cost is (900 − 750)×2 = 300; unused setup cost is (20 − 14)×30 = 180. Assigned 1,920 plus unused 480 equals the supplied 2,400. Removing Y would leave its assigned resources unused; the immediate saving in these committed pools is zero. Cancellable contracts, fewer paid shifts, a separable resource sale or another feasible profitable use could change the decision. Each needs evidence about the amount, timing and consequences; allocation alone supplies none.
  4. At 310 hours, (80,30) uses all hours and 8 + 15 = 23 setups. The bound 30x + 60y = 12(2x + 5y) + 6x ≤ 12×310 + 6×80 = 4,200 is attained, proving the unique optimum. Gross improvement over 4,080 is 120; after fee 150 the incremental benefit is −30, so reject the expansion under these facts. At 400 hours, the setup bound gives contribution at most 3,600 + 18×80 = 5,040, attained uniquely by (80,44), using 380 hours and 30 setups. Profit before any expansion fee is 2,040. The gross improvement over baseline is 960, not 12×100 = 1,200. Once setups bind, some additional machine capacity is unusable for profitable feasible output.
  5. Own contribution is 6(45 − 18) = 162. Subtract preparation 36 and displaced contribution 3×40 = 120, giving incremental profit 6; accept on the stated monetary terms. Break-even quote is 18 + (36 + 120)/6 = 44. With the extra penalty, the increment is −14 and the quote threshold is 18 + (36 + 120 + 20)/6 = 142/3, about 47.333; reject at 45. With genuine spare capacity and no displaced orders, the original increment is 162 − 36 = 126 and quote threshold 24. The penalty, if still applicable in that idle context, reduces the increment to 106. These comparisons do not infer opportunity cost from an overhead rate.
  6. Relevant make cash is 50×8 + 200 = 600; purchase plus shipping is 50×13 + 100 = 750. Buying earns the alternative 180, so its net advantage is 600 − 750 + 180 = 30. The quote condition 50p + 100 ≤ 600 + 180 gives p ≤ 13.6. Depreciation, unchanged common cash and past design expenditure do not enter this difference. With incremental resale proceeds 30, buying's advantage becomes 60 and its threshold becomes (600 + 180 + 30 − 100)/50 = 14.2. The 30 is a future consequence of the choice, unlike the historical purchase amount. Under the specified no-tax case, a book disposal gain or loss is not a second cash consequence to add to those proceeds.
  7. The fixed manufacturing rate is 10 per unit. Absorption unit manufacturing cost is 30, so sold-unit cost is 90×30 = 2,700 and closing inventory 30×30 = 900. Profit is 4,500 − 2,700 − 360 − 300 = 1,140. Variable-cost closing inventory is 30×20 = 600; profit is 4,500 − 1,800 − 1,200 − 360 − 300 = 840. Actual operating cash is 4,500 − 2,400 − 1,200 − 360 − 300 = 240. The bridges are 1,140 − 900 = 240 and 840 − 600 = 240. Profit differs by 300, the fixed manufacturing amount retained in the 30 unsold units. It is an expense-timing difference under the supplied conventions, not a cash receipt or an endorsement of unnecessary production.
  8. Expected incremental rework cost is (1/4)×1,200 = 300. Expected private benefit is 400 − 300 = 100; including expected resident harm gives incremental net social benefit 100 − 150 = −50, assuming all other consequences were already counted. The positive private expectation does not establish admissibility: the required certification is a separate constraint and has not been documented. Nor does risk neutrality guarantee that a 1,200 payment in the bad state is fundable. Relevant missing facts include verified compliant quality, reliable on-time delivery, actual cancellability of supervision, and whether the alternative job can really use the released resources and earn its stated net contribution. Any two, explained, satisfy the final request.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back task. In four minutes, explain to an operations manager why Meridian's allocated P loss does not justify dropping P, why the busy special-order threshold differs from the idle threshold, and why unused capacity cost is not automatically a cash saving. Give one way an integer or second-resource constraint changes a marginal-value argument.

Teach-back benchmark

The single-rate baseline assigns 1,500 to P and reports a product loss of 60, but P contributes 1,440 toward fixed commitments that remain even if it is removed. In the idle context the special order needs only its new variable cost and 40 external payment, producing threshold 74. In the busy context it displaces the best regular use of 20 hours, worth 240, raising the threshold to 98. ABC separates assigned use from 720 of unused capacity cost, but the contracts still require payment. A released resource saves money only when supply can change or another benefit is realized. At 301 hours integer quantities give no contribution improvement; at 400 hours the setup ceiling limits the optimum to (80,44), so a single constant machine-hour value cannot describe every expansion.

Delayed check, 7–14 days later. Change only P's variable cost in the original main case from 100 to 110. Keep demand, hours, batches, fixed pools and all special-order terms unchanged. Find and prove the new optimal quantities, contribution and profit. Then find the busy special order's displaced contribution, incremental profit and break-even quote. Explain whether ABC driver rates change.

Delayed-check answer

P now contributes 50 per unit. For every feasible plan, 30x + 50y = 10(2x + 5y) + 10x ≤ 10×300 + 10×80 = 3,800. The feasible (80,28) attains the bound uniquely, so contribution is 3,800 and profit 800. Reserving 20 hours still leaves optimal regular quantities (80,24), losing four P contributions of 50, or 200. The special order increment is 150 − 40 − 200 = −90; its threshold is 70 + (40 + 200)/10 = 94. Pool costs and practical-capacity denominators did not change, so ABC rates remain 6 per hour and 30 per setup. Changing a product's direct variable cost changes contribution, not those supplied overhead rates.

Next step. Financial ratios and business diagnosis uses reported margins, turnover and returns. Carry forward the question of which allocation, capacity denominator, inventory policy and decision horizon produced each number.
